title: The Concept of Childhood in Western Countries

source.filename: Practice 54  IETLS 閱讀練習 - Passage 1.pdf

paragraphs.text: The Concept of Childhood in Western Countries The history of childhood has been a prominent topic in social history since the influential book Centuries of Childhood, written by the French historian Philippe Ariès, appeared in 1960. Ariès claimed that ‘childhood’ is a concept created by modern society.

Whether childhood itself is a recent invention is one of the most intensely debated issues in its history. Philippe Ariès argued that during the Middle Ages, up to about the end of the 15th century, children in Western Europe were regarded as miniature adults, with all the intellect and personality that this implied. After examining medieval pictures and diaries, he concluded that children and adults were not clearly distinguished because they shared similar work and leisure activities. However, he argued, this did not mean that children were neglected, abandoned or despised. The idea of childhood reflects an awareness of childhood’s distinctive nature, which separates a child from an adult or even a young adult. The concept should not be confused with affection for children.

Traditionally, children played a functional role by contributing to family income and were therefore considered useful. In the Middle Ages, children of five or six performed necessary chores for their parents. During the 16th century, those aged nine or ten were often encouraged, or even forced, to leave home to work as servants for wealthier families or as apprentices learning a trade.

In the 18th and 19th centuries, industrialisation created new demand for child labour, forcing many children to work long hours in mines, workshops and factories. Whether such labour interfered with their physical growth began to concern social reformers, some of whom recognised the potential of systematic studies to measure how these early deprivations affected development.

Reformers’ concerns gradually improved children’s working conditions. In Britain, for example, the Factory Act of 1833 marked the emergence of legal protection against exploitation and was associated with the rise of schools for factory children. Factory reform gradually eliminated the worst abuses, while trade unions and economic change also helped by making some forms of child labour redundant during the 19th century. Initiating children into work was no longer the priority, and play and education came to be regarded as appropriate for all children rather than only a privileged minority. Childhood was increasingly understood as an extended period of dependency, development and learning, while the age at which full-time work began was delayed. Even so, work retained a significant, if less essential, role in children’s lives during the late 19th and 20th centuries. In the first decade of the 21st century, the ‘useful child’ became controversial, especially amid global concern about the many children still engaged in labour.

The half-time schools established under the Factory Act of 1833 allowed children to work and attend school. However, a significant proportion of children did not attend school in the 1840s, and many of those who did dropped out by the age of 10 or 11. By the end of the 19th century in Britain, the situation changed dramatically, and schools became central to the concept of a ‘normal’ childhood.

School attendance is no longer a privilege, and every child is expected to spend a substantial part of the day in a classroom. School separates children’s lives from domestic life and the adult world of work, becoming an institution devoted to shaping young people’s minds, behaviour and morals. Education also dominates children’s waking hours through classroom time, homework, the growth of after-school activities and the importance attached to parental involvement.

Industrialisation, urbanisation and mass schooling created new challenges for those responsible for protecting children’s welfare and promoting learning. Increasingly, children are treated as a group with distinctive needs and organised according to age. Teachers, for example, need to know what to expect from children, which instruction suits different age groups and how best to assess progress. They also require tools for sorting and selecting children according to ability and potential.
